faq_h2: Questions LED tube makers ask about this line
q1: Can 8 or 10 mm bare strips run through the line directly?
a1: No. The strips ride in carriers of 12–16 strips through every station; carrier design is approved before the line is built.
a2: No. It is the placer's published optimum rate. The line target is 300 good strips an hour, confirmed in an 8-hour capacity trial.
q3: How many strips a month can the line make?
a3: At 26 days × 16 hours and 300 good strips an hour, 124,800 strips a month before downstream lamp-assembly losses.
q4: How many operators does it need?
a4: The initial estimate is 3–4 operators per shift, with 30–60 minute changeovers inside the approved product family.
q5: What space and utilities are needed?
a5: About 22.0 m of machine bodies; plan about 25 × 5 m. 220 V for auxiliaries, 380 V three-phase for placer and oven, compressed air and reflow exhaust.
q6: What do you need from us for a firm proposal?
a6: Final Gerber, BOM and LED circuit for both strip widths. We return the carrier design, a sample run and the confirmed configuration.
bl1t: Why 1.2 m LED strips break ordinary SMT lines
bl1s: What changes when the board is 1,170 mm long and 8 mm wide.
bl1p1: Put a 1,170 mm LED strip on a standard SMT conveyor and it sags, twists or falls between rails before it reaches the printer.
bl1p2: Most lines are built for boards under 500 mm, so long, narrow LED strips end up hand-placed or run on machines that stop every few boards.
bl1p3: Treat length as the first design input: every station from loader to unloader must carry 1,200 mm, and the strips must ride in carriers rather than on bare rails.
bl1p4: This line is sized that way: SM-VL1200 loader, SM-1200 printer, SM-F7S placer up to 1,200 × 330 mm, SM-CVB1200 buffer, SM-AI1251 AOI and SM-UL1200 unloader.
bl1p5: Check every new strip length against the 1,200 mm envelope before you quote the job.
bl1p6: Send us your strip drawing and we will check it against each station.
bl2t: Carriers decide your LED line speed
bl2s: Why the carrier design comes before the machine list.
bl2p1: On an LED tube line, the carrier is the product the machines actually see.
bl2p2: Teams often buy machines first and design carriers later, then find the carrier does not fit the buffer pitch or the unloader width.
bl2p3: Design the carrier against all stations at once: envelope, thickness, weight, flatness, heat expansion and strips per carrier.
bl2p4: Here the target envelope is ≤1,200 × 250 mm with 12–16 strips per carrier, leaving only 30 mm for end features; 40 carriers start the line.
bl2p5: Review carrier wear and flatness on a schedule; a warped carrier shows up as print and placement defects.
bl2p6: Ask us for the carrier design review for your strips.
bl3t: How many strips a month: the simple capacity sum
bl3s: Turning a monthly target into an hourly line rate.
bl3p1: "100,000 strips a month" sounds clear until you ask how many hours the line runs.
bl3p2: Without the hours, a buyer cannot tell whether one line on one shift is enough.
bl3p3: Divide the monthly target by scheduled hours, then add margin for effectiveness and yield.
bl3p4: With 26 days × 16 hours = 416 hours, 100,000 strips needs 240.4 good strips an hour; the line targets 300, giving 124,800 a month. One 8-hour shift would need 480.8 an hour.
bl3p5: Redo the sum whenever your shift pattern or monthly target changes.
bl3p6: Share your monthly target and shifts; we will size the line to it.
bl4t: Reading a 180,000 CPH placer rate correctly
bl4s: Why the brochure rate is not your line output.
bl4p1: A 180,000 CPH number on a brochure is exciting, and misleading if read as output.
bl4p2: Published rates are optimum conditions; real output depends on LED count, carrier changes and line effectiveness.
bl4p3: Work back from strips: LEDs per strip × strips per hour = net placements; divide by effectiveness for the ideal rate the placer must reach.
bl4p4: At 300 good 120-LED strips an hour the line needs 36,000 net placements an hour, 48,000 at 75 % effectiveness, well inside the SM-F7S published 180,000 CPH.
bl4p5: Confirm the real cycle at FAT with your own strips and both recipes.
bl4p6: Ask us for the placement sum for your LED counts.
bl5t: Reflow and cooling for long aluminium strips
bl5s: Getting heat in and out of 1,170 mm boards.
bl5p1: Aluminium LED strips carry heat well, which is exactly why they are hard to profile.
bl5p2: A profile set on air temperature alone can leave LEDs under-soldered on MCPCB or overheated on FR4.
bl5p3: Profile the loaded carrier, not the oven: thermocouples on the strip, both materials, full load, then cool before inspection.
bl5p4: This line uses SM-R733 with 10 top / 10 bottom heating zones and 3 cooling zones, an 8-channel SM-TP8 profiler, and the SM-CVB1200 buffer before AOI.
bl5p5: Re-profile when paste, LED or board material changes.
bl5p6: Send your paste and LED data for a starting profile.
bl6t: What AOI should catch on LED strips
bl6s: Polarity, missing LEDs and solder defects.
bl6p1: One reversed LED makes a whole tube fail at light-up.
bl6p2: Visual checks by operators miss defects on long strips late in a shift.
bl6p3: Define the defects first: polarity, missing or shifted LEDs, visible solder faults; then agree false-call and escape limits with seeded samples.
bl6p4: The SM-AI1251 inspects up to 1,200 × 510 mm with a 12 MP camera at 15 µm; its acceptance uses known-good and seeded-defect samples on FR4 and MCPCB.
bl6p5: Review false calls weekly and tune the program as LED suppliers change.
bl6p6: Ask for an AOI sample run on your strips.
bl7t: Planning floor space and utilities for an LED line
bl7s: What to prepare before the machines arrive.
bl7p1: Machines arrive on time more often than the floor is ready for them.
bl7p2: Missing three-phase power, air or exhaust delays start-up by weeks.
bl7p3: List each machine's body length, power, air and exhaust, then add access, carrier handling and return routes.
bl7p4: This line is about 22.0 m of machine bodies; plan about 25 × 5 m, 220 V auxiliaries, 380 V three-phase for placer and oven, 0.49 MPa air, and reflow exhaust.
bl7p5: Update the site plan when options such as 3D SPI are added.
bl7p6: Ask us for the utility schedule for your floor.
bl8t: From quotation to a running LED line in seven stages
bl8s: A clear acceptance path for buyer and supplier.
bl8p1: A line is only as good as the way it is accepted.
bl8p2: Vague acceptance leads to disputes over output and quality after shipment.
bl8p3: Agree seven stages: design review, dry-run handling, print and placement, reflow and cooling, AOI validation, capacity trial, site acceptance and training.
bl8p4: The capacity trial runs one full 8-hour shift on the bottleneck product, logging good output, rejects, operators and stops against 300 good strips an hour.
bl8p5: Keep the same logs after start-up to track the line month by month.
bl8p6: Send your product data to start the design review.
